A method to calculate normals for hexahedral meshes using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals, converted from computational space to physical space via the Jacobian matrix [S1].

The claim is explicitly supported by the text in Section 5.3 'Normal Calculation'. The text states: 'If we assume for a moment, that we know the normal vectors at each of the eight vertices of a hexahedron we can proceed as follows... This corresponds to a kind of trilinear interpolation.' It further explains: 'The basic idea is to compute the normal like in a regular grid with unit length, i.e. in computational space. The following relationship can thereafter be used to convert between physical coordinates xi and computational coordinates... determined using the Jacobian matrix Jij'. It concludes with: 'Hence we can calculate three vectors... A linear combination of these vectors with the normal in computational space Nc results in the converted normal Np.' This matches the claim's description of using trilinear interpolation of vertex normals and converting via the Jacobian matrix.

*   **Holes in Hexahedron:** Bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points [S1].

The claim states that bilinear patches are generally not flat, introducing holes in the hexahedron because the implicit edge representation depends on all four face vertices, unlike Plücker coordinates which depend solely on two edge points. This is explicitly stated in the provided text under section '5.1.2. Bilinear Patch-Extension': 'However, in some configurations this is not possible since bilinear patches are generally not flat, i.e. we introduce holes in our hexahedron. These holes are caused by the implicit edge representation of bilinear patches. In particular, an edge of the bilinear patch depends on all four face vertices. In contrast, Plücker coordinates allow a unique decision whether a ray passes clockwise or counter-clockwise since they depend solely on the two edge points.'
